accuracy.reason: All eight objectives hold under the explicitly scoped S3/GCS standard object model. Namespace, separate database commits, old-or-new replacement, listing limits, uncertain responses, retention and authorization boundaries match live primary documentation.

evidence.quote: Complete old or new bytes is one guarantee; retaining both is another.

mechanisms.reason: The stack traces bucket/key retrieval, separate publication failures, replacement races, conditional checks and lost acknowledgments, redundancy versus configured recovery, and credential versus application ownership decisions. The two diagrams correctly separate upload/publication and existence/intended-content evidence.

evidence.quote: Finding the key proves only that some object exists.

coherence.reason: Object/key/metadata precede upload/reference coordination, replacement and lists; these prerequisites support retries, durability and access, then five interface choices. All eight card objectives are developed without assuming a recurring story.

evidence.quote: The object upload and database commit are separate operations.

decisions.reason: The reader can defer ready publication, reconcile unreferenced objects, protect replacements conditionally, select retention and permissions, and choose database/block/file/CDN responsibilities by access pattern. Costs include listing growth, whole-object edits and application recovery.

evidence.quote: Whole-object replacement and request overhead make it a poor default for frequent small in-place edits.

clarity.reason: Definitions and scoped examples support the stated HTTP/API prerequisites. The listing and conditional-retry cards are dense but explicit; diagrams reinforce the important distinctions. Shared renderer/CSS inspected, no browser execution claimed.

evidence.quote: The bucket and key locate an object; the application gives its bytes meaning.

outcomes.reason: Learner defines bucket/object/key/metadata, scoped flat prefixes and non-atomic rename; traces reference-based retrieval and separate commits with publication ordering and both failure recoveries.
Learner explains complete replacement, S3/GCS atomic old-or-new reads/current value, concurrent overlap and separately configured historical retention.

Learner distinguishes exact lookup, prefix enumeration and indexed field queries; costs, provider-scoped consistency, failure/cache boundaries, pagination, multi-key limits and concurrent acknowledgment ambiguity are supported.

Learner traces uncertain completion and destructive unconditional retry; distinguishes identity/content from existence and later observation from original outcome; conditional protections and rejection/lost-response limits are supported.
Learner separates durability, availability and response receipt; explains redundancy, placement/zone limits, deletion/replacement and enabled/effective/retained recovery protections.
Learner covers credential authorization versus user ownership, opaque keys, least privilege and revocation delays, all five storage/delivery roles, small-object allowance and whole-object tradeoffs.

sourceChecks.claim: Live inspected S3 object-key flat-namespace section and GCS object namespace/rename followup: prefixes are name characters and simulated-directory rename copies/deletes individual objects non-atomically.

Live inspected S3 introduction and consistency section: objects use bucket/key metadata; atomicity is key-scoped, not a database transaction. The lesson publication/reconciliation steps are appropriate application-level consequences of separate commits.

Live inspected GCS object immutability/replacement and S3 single-key atomicity: complete old/new reads, current replacement and separately configured versions. Scope excludes other specialized interfaces.

Live inspected GCS consistency and S3 consistency/concurrent application sections; followed GCS list API pageToken documentation, which permits changes between pages. Strong reads/lists neither guarantee availability nor a cross-key/database transaction.

Live inspected GCS generation preconditions and retry races, and S3 conditional-write followup. Existence checks protect live keys, matching conditions protect expected state, and rejection is not evidence of intended content.

Live inspected GCS durability page: redundant storage precedes success confirmation and zonal failures may lose locally redundant data. S3 protection/consistency followups support stored successful writes, class-dependent placement and version recovery; response delivery remains separate.

Live inspected GCS IAM principals, roles and resource scopes; GCS consistency explicitly documents delayed access revocation. A service credential does not imply application user ownership, so application authorization remains necessary.

Live inspected AWS block/file/object comparison and CloudFront introduction followup: file/block/key interfaces differ; an edge cache fetches authoritative origin bytes, including S3 origins. Prior inspected block-source facts support disk-like range operations.
